result.overall: The judicial review application by the Minister is allowed because the Board member erred in granting an extension of time for appeal without sufficient reasons and without considering prejudice to the Minister.

themes.name: Extension of time criteria
themes.summary: The decision to grant an extension of time must consider continuing intention to pursue, arguable case, reasonable explanation for delay, and absence of prejudice.

themes.name: Respondent's reasons for delay
themes.summary: The Respondent's explanations for the delay were inconsistent, unsupported, and unreasonable.

themes.name: Prejudice to the Minister
themes.summary: The Board failed to consider potential prejudice to the Minister from the long delay in appealing.

themes.name: Procedural fairness and ex parte decision
themes.summary: The decision was made without notice or submissions from the Minister, raising concerns about fairness.

arguments.quote: The Minister alleges that the member designate of the Board erred in granting (a) an extension of time and (b) leave to appeal.
arguments.claim: The member designate of the Board erred in granting an extension of time.

arguments.quote: The Minister alleges that the member designate of the Board erred in granting (a) an extension of time and (b) leave to appeal. In the circumstances of this case, I must agree with the Minister and allow this application on the basis that the member erred in extending the time for bringing the appeal.
arguments.claim: The member designate of the Board erred in granting leave to appeal.
arguments.outcome_note: The Court only explicitly agrees on the error in extending time, not on leave to appeal.

arguments.quote: The Applicant submits that, in spite of this discretionary nature of the decision, I should apply a standard of review of reasonableness simpliciter (Callihoo v. Canada, [2000] F.C.J. No. 612 (T.D.)).
arguments.claim: The standard of review for the decision to extend time and grant leave should be reasonableness simpliciter.

arguments.quote: Jurisprudence relied on by the Minister (Grewal v. Canada (Minister of Employment and Immigration), [1985] 2 F.C. 263 (F.C.A.); Baksa v. Neis (c.o.b. Brookside Transport), [2002] F.C.J. No. 832) has established that the following criteria must be considered and weighed: 1. A continuing intention to pursue the application or appeal; 2. The matter discloses an arguable case; 3. There is a reasonable explanation for the delay; and 4. There is no prejudice to the other party in allowing the extension.
arguments.claim: The Minister relies on jurisprudence establishing criteria for extension of time: continuing intention to pursue, arguable case, reasonable explanation for delay, and no prejudice to other party.

arguments.quote: Her reasons, as set out in her initial letter to the Board dated February 8, 2004, were as follows: Ms. Gattellaro did not act earlier on this due to many difficulties in her life. She was having to cope with her significant depression, her marital problems and raising her young children. And the process for the Pension Appeals Board was not properly communicated to her for her full understanding of the situation.
arguments.claim: The Respondent provided reasons for delay including significant depression, marital problems, raising young children, and lack of proper communication about the Pension Appeals Board process.

arguments.quote: Mrs. Gattellaro was in such a state of depression that she could not take care of her affairs regarding appealing the decision from the Review Tribunal. Her former representative abandoned her case. And Mrs. Gattellaro's husband came across the documentation and persuaded her to pursue her case and that he would provide the support she required.
arguments.claim: In a second letter, the Respondent stated she was in such a state of depression that she could not manage her affairs, her former representative abandoned her case, and her husband persuaded her to pursue the appeal and support her.

arguments.quote: It is difficult to see how the Board can reach a fair, principled decision on these applications on an ex parte basis; that is, without the submissions from the Minister.
arguments.claim: It is difficult to see how the Board can reach a fair, principled decision on these applications on an ex parte basis; that is, without the submissions from the Minister.

arguments.quote: The Minister does not seek costs.
arguments.claim: The Minister does not seek costs.

holdings.quote: This is an application by the Minister of Human Resources Development (the "Minister") for judicial review of the October 22, 2004 decision by a member of the Pension Appeal Board (the "Board"), designated under s. 83(2.1) of the Canada Pension Plan, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-8 (the "CPP").
holdings.statement: The Minister applied for judicial review of the October 22, 2004 decision by a member of the Pension Appeal Board under s. 83(2.1) of the Canada Pension Plan.

holdings.quote: In his decision, the designated member granted the Respondent an extension of time and leave to appeal a decision of the Review Tribunal approximately seven and a half years after the time limit for doing so had expired.
holdings.statement: The Board member granted the Respondent an extension of time and leave to appeal a Review Tribunal decision about seven and a half years after the deadline had expired.

holdings.quote: While the Respondent, who was self-represented, filed no materials for this application, she appeared and made oral representations at the hearing.
holdings.statement: The Respondent was self-represented, filed no materials for the application, but appeared and made oral representations at the hearing.

holdings.quote: The sequence of events leading to this application is as follows: _ The Respondent applied for disability benefits in July 1995. _ Her application was denied in July 1995, and after reconsideration the denial was confirmed by letter decision dated March 29, 1996. _ The Respondent appealed the decision to a Review Tribunal who, in reasons dated February 26, 1997, dismissed her appeal.
holdings.statement: The Respondent applied for disability benefits in July 1995, was denied, and the denial was confirmed after reconsideration in March 1996.

holdings.quote: The sequence of events leading to this application is as follows: _ The Respondent applied for disability benefits in July 1995. _ Her application was denied in July 1995, and after reconsideration the denial was confirmed by letter decision dated March 29, 1996. _ The Respondent appealed the decision to a Review Tribunal who, in reasons dated February 26, 1997, dismissed her appeal. The Review Tribunal concluded that the Respondent was "capable of doing some type of work suited to her disabilities". _ In letters to the Board dated February 11, 2004 and May 3, 2004, the Respondent requested an extension of time and leave to appeal the Review Tribunal's decision of February 26, 1997. _ On October 22, 2004, in a Notice of Decision from the Board, the Respondent was advised that, the time within which to appeal was extended and the leave to appeal was granted.
holdings.statement: The Respondent appealed to a Review Tribunal which dismissed her appeal in February 1997, concluding she was capable of some work suited to her disabilities.

holdings.quote: The Review Tribunal concluded that the Respondent was "capable of doing some type of work suited to her disabilities". _ In letters to the Board dated February 11, 2004 and May 3, 2004, the Respondent requested an extension of time and leave to appeal the Review Tribunal's decision of February 26, 1997. _ On October 22, 2004, in a Notice of Decision from the Board, the Respondent was advised that, the time within which to appeal was extended and the leave to appeal was granted.
holdings.statement: The Respondent requested an extension of time and leave to appeal the Review Tribunal's decision in letters dated February 11, 2004 and May 3, 2004.

holdings.quote: The Review Tribunal concluded that the Respondent was "capable of doing some type of work suited to her disabilities". _ In letters to the Board dated February 11, 2004 and May 3, 2004, the Respondent requested an extension of time and leave to appeal the Review Tribunal's decision of February 26, 1997. _ On October 22, 2004, in a Notice of Decision from the Board, the Respondent was advised that, the time within which to appeal was extended and the leave to appeal was granted. No reasons were provided. Further, the decision was taken ex parte, without notice to or submissions from the Minister.
holdings.statement: On October 22, 2004, the Board extended the time to appeal and granted leave to appeal, but provided no reasons and made the decision ex parte without notice to the Minister.

holdings.quote: In the circumstances of this case, I must agree with the Minister and allow this application on the basis that the member erred in extending the time for bringing the appeal.
holdings.statement: The member erred in extending the time for bringing the appeal and the application is allowed on that basis.

holdings.quote: In this case, I do not need to reach a conclusion on the appropriate standard since I am satisfied that, on any standard of review, the decision should not stand.
holdings.statement: The court does not need to decide the appropriate standard of review because the decision should not stand under any standard.

holdings.quote: The decision of the designated member to extend time and to grant leave is highly discretionary.
holdings.statement: The decision to extend time and grant leave is highly discretionary.

holdings.quote: (1) A party or, subject to the regulations, any person on behalf thereof, or the Minister, if dissatisfied with a decision of a Review Tribunal made under section 82, other than a decision made in respect of an appeal referred to in subsection 28(1) of the Old Age Security Act, or under subsection 84(2), may, within ninety days after the day on which that decision was communicated to the party or Minister, or within such longer period as the Chairman or Vice-Chairman of the Pension Appeals Board may either before or after the expiration of those ninety days allow, apply in writing to the Chairman or Vice-Chairman for leave to appeal that decision to the Pension Appeals Board. 83.
holdings.statement: Section 83(1) of the CPP limits the time for bringing an appeal of a Review Tribunal decision to ninety days after the decision is communicated, subject to extension by the Chairman or Vice-Chairman of the Pension Appeals Board.

holdings.quote: The procedure for appeals brought pursuant to s. 83 of the CPP is dealt with in Rules 4 and 5 of the Rules of Procedure of the Board (C.R.C. 1978, c. 390, as amended). Read together, these Rules provide that an application for an extension of time within which to apply for leave to appeal a decision of a Review Tribunal shall set out the date of the decision of the Review Tribunal, the place at which the Tribunal's decision was rendered, the date on which the decision was communicated to the appellant, the full name and postal address of the appellant, the name and address of any agent or representative of the appellant on whom service of documents may be made, the grounds upon which the appellant relies to obtain leave to appeal, a statement of the appellant's allegations of fact, reference to any statutory provisions relied on and, reasons the appellant intends to submit and documentary evidence the appellant intends to rely on in support of the appeal.
holdings.statement: The procedure for appeals under s. 83 of the CPP is governed by Rules 4 and 5 of the Rules of Procedure of the Board, which require an application for extension of time to include specific information such as the date and place of the Review Tribunal decision, communication date, appellant's details, grounds for leave to appeal, allegations of fact, statutory references, reasons, and documentary evidence.

holdings.quote: The application should also set out the grounds on which the extension of time is sought.
holdings.statement: An application for extension of time must also set out the grounds on which the extension is sought.

holdings.quote: The intent of Parliament as expressed in s. 83(1) of the CPP is to limit the time period for extending the appeal period to 90 days.
holdings.statement: The intent of Parliament in s. 83(1) of the CPP is to limit the extension of the appeal period to 90 days.

holdings.quote: While a designated member may extend the time period beyond 90 days, it must be presumed that an extension of time is not a matter of right. If the Board grants extensions automatically - which appears to be the case in this application - the 90-day limit becomes meaningless. The authority to extend the statutory limitation must not, in my view, be exercised arbitrarily or capriciously.
holdings.statement: An extension of time beyond 90 days is not a matter of right and must not be granted automatically or arbitrarily.

holdings.quote: The question becomes, under what circumstances should an extension of time be granted? In other words, what factors should be weighed in determining whether to grant an extension of time?
holdings.statement: The question is under what circumstances an extension of time should be granted and what factors should be weighed in that determination.

holdings.quote: The situation faced by a member of the Board considering a request is analogous to that before a judge of the Federal Court in considering an extension of time for bringing an application for judicial review pursuant to s. 18.1(2) of the Federal Courts Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. F-7, as amended. That provision of the Federal Courts Act provides that an application for judicial review is to be made within 30 days "or within any further time that a judge of the Federal Court may fix or allow". The wording is almost identical to the relevant provision in the CPP. Also similar to the CPP, there is no statutory duty on a judge to give reasons for a decision to allow an extension of time. Thus, in my view, it is reasonable that the same principles applicable to a judge of the Federal Court ought to be engaged on a decision to extend time made by a member of the Board.
holdings.statement: The principles applicable to a Federal Court judge considering an extension of time under s. 18.1(2) of the Federal Courts Act are reasonably applicable to a Board member deciding on an extension of time under the CPP.

holdings.quote: They are, in my view, equally applicable to the decision under review.
holdings.statement: The criteria from the jurisprudence are equally applicable to the decision under review.

holdings.quote: I note that the decision to extend the time period has been made without submissions by the Minister, a party equally affected by the decision to proceed to an appeal. In light of this, it seems even more critical in the interests of justice, that the record demonstrates clearly that all of these factors have been addressed by the decision maker.
holdings.statement: It is critical in the interests of justice that the record clearly demonstrates that all these factors have been addressed by the decision maker, especially since the Minister was not given an opportunity to make submissions.

holdings.quote: This is not to say that this Court should intervene lightly in a decision of the designated member of the Board. Provided that the record demonstrates that there was a reasonable evidentiary basis upon which the member could assess the factors, it would not be up to this Court to re-weigh the evidence.
holdings.statement: The Court should not lightly intervene in a Board member's decision to extend time if there is a reasonable evidentiary basis to assess the factors and the Court should not re-weigh the evidence.

holdings.quote: In the case before me, I am prepared to assume, without deciding, that the first two criteria have been met.
holdings.statement: I am prepared to assume, without deciding, that the first two criteria for extension of time have been met.

holdings.quote: However, I have serious concerns with respect to the last two factors of explanation for the delay and prejudice to the Minister.
holdings.statement: I have serious concerns with respect to the last two factors of explanation for the delay and prejudice to the Minister.

holdings.quote: The Respondent provided no affidavit to support her position on this judicial review.
holdings.statement: The Respondent provided no affidavit to support her position on this judicial review.

holdings.quote: A review of the record demonstrates that her reasons do not hold up to scrutiny. 1.
holdings.statement: The reasons given by the Respondent do not hold up to scrutiny based on the record.

holdings.quote: Young children. The only evidence with respect to her children is that they were born in 1968 and 1970. At the time of the decision in question, they were 29 and 27 years of age and not, as she alleged, "young children". 2.
holdings.statement: The Respondent's children were born in 1968 and 1970 and were therefore adults at the time of the decision, not young children as alleged.

holdings.quote: Further, there is no support for her statement that she was "abandoned" by her representative. The record indicates that the person who represented her at the Review Tribunal was still acting as her representative at the time the Notice of Decision of Review Tribunal was sent to both the Respondent and her representative. That Notice clearly spelled out the time limitation for an appeal. 3.
holdings.statement: There is no support for the statement that the Respondent was abandoned by her representative; the representative was still acting at the time the Notice of Decision was sent, which clearly stated the time limit for appeal.

holdings.quote: In spite of claimed "difficulties", the Respondent initiated a second application for disability benefits in 1999. The fact that she was able to bring a second application followed by an application for reconsideration and an appeal to the Review Tribunal, all of which were denied, raises a serious question of the truth of her statements that she was unable to act earlier due to her difficulties and depression. 4.
holdings.statement: Despite claimed difficulties, the Respondent initiated a second application for disability benefits in 1999 and subsequent appeals, raising serious questions about the truth of her statements that she was unable to act earlier due to her difficulties and depression.

holdings.quote: Marital Difficulty. While she first described marital difficulties as a reason for delay, in the second letter, her husband was described as providing support in her appeal.
holdings.statement: While marital difficulties were initially cited as a reason for delay, the Respondent later described her husband as providing support in her appeal.

holdings.quote: No correspondence is contained in the record indicating that the Board requested clarification of these inconsistencies.
holdings.statement: No correspondence in the record indicates that the Board requested clarification of inconsistencies in the Respondent's reasons for delay.

holdings.quote: A conclusion that the Respondent has provided compelling or sufficient reasons for bringing the leave application seven years after the 90-day time limit of s. 83(1) is, in my view, totally unsupported by the evidence and is patently unreasonable.
holdings.statement: A conclusion that the Respondent has provided compelling or sufficient reasons for bringing the leave application seven years late is totally unsupported by the evidence and patently unreasonable.

holdings.quote: With respect to the fourth factor, the record discloses no evidence whatsoever on the question of prejudice to the Minister. It does not appear that prejudice to the Minister was considered by the member.
holdings.statement: There is no evidence on the question of prejudice to the Minister, and it does not appear that prejudice was considered by the member.

holdings.quote: Given that there has been over seven years since the original decision and an even longer time since the Respondent made her initial application for CPP disability benefits, how is the Minister to ensure that an adequate response to the appeal is made? This could make the extension of time very prejudicial to the Minister.
holdings.statement: Given the long delay, it is difficult for the Minister to ensure an adequate response to the appeal, which could make the extension of time very prejudicial to the Minister.

holdings.quote: In a more general sense of the concept of prejudice, I am also concerned that allowing appeals, absent compelling reasons, long after the expiry of time leads to a lack of certainty and finality for both the Minister and all parties to the process.
holdings.statement: Allowing appeals long after expiry of time without compelling reasons leads to lack of certainty and finality for the Minister and all parties.

holdings.quote: It is reasonable to assume that there are many other persons who, having received negative decisions of the Review Tribunal, have not appealed based on the expiry of time. The Respondent should not now be allowed to pursue a remedy that others in her position have not pursued believing that an appeal was not open to them.
holdings.statement: Many persons with negative Review Tribunal decisions have not appealed due to expiry of time, and the Respondent should not be allowed to pursue a remedy that others have not pursued believing appeal was closed.

holdings.quote: There is fundamental unfairness in a process that is not applied consistently and with regard to commonly accepted principles.
holdings.statement: It is fundamentally unfair to have a process that is not applied consistently and with regard to commonly accepted principles.

holdings.quote: An application for an extension of time - particularly for seven years beyond the statutory time limit - should not be granted as a matter of right, but should be subjected to a principled approach by the Board.
holdings.statement: An application for an extension of time, especially for seven years beyond the statutory limit, should be subjected to a principled approach by the Board and not granted as a matter of right.

holdings.quote: In this case, that was not done. In conclusion, I am of the view that the member erred in extending the time for bringing the appeal and, accordingly, this application for judicial review will be allowed.
holdings.statement: The Board member erred in extending the time for bringing the appeal without applying a principled approach.

holdings.quote: In conclusion, I am of the view that the member erred in extending the time for bringing the appeal and, accordingly, this application for judicial review will be allowed. The decision under review will be set aside and the matter referred back to the Board for re-determination, having regard to these reasons, by a different member of the Board.
holdings.statement: This application for judicial review is allowed and the decision under review is set aside.

holdings.quote: The decision under review will be set aside and the matter referred back to the Board for re-determination, having regard to these reasons, by a different member of the Board. In particular, the member designated to consider the application for the extension of time should satisfy himself that: _ The Respondent demonstrates a continuing intention to pursue the application or appeal; _ The matter discloses an arguable case; _ There is a reasonable explanation for the delay; and _ There is no prejudice to the Minister in allowing the extension.
holdings.statement: The matter is referred back to the Board for re-determination by a different member, who must consider the application for extension of time according to specified criteria.

holdings.quote: In particular, the member designated to consider the application for the extension of time should satisfy himself that: _ The Respondent demonstrates a continuing intention to pursue the application or appeal; _ The matter discloses an arguable case; _ There is a reasonable explanation for the delay; and _ There is no prejudice to the Minister in allowing the extension.
holdings.statement: The member designated to consider the extension of time must ensure that the Respondent demonstrates a continuing intention to pursue the appeal, that the matter discloses an arguable case, that there is a reasonable explanation for the delay, and that there is no prejudice to the Minister in allowing the extension.

holdings.quote: In spite of this concern, I recognize that the Board is the master of its own procedures and, therefore, decline to require the Board to implement procedures that would address these shortcomings.
holdings.statement: The Board is the master of its own procedures and the Court declines to require the Board to implement procedures that would address these shortcomings.

holdings.quote: In my discretion, I decline to award costs in this application.
holdings.statement: I decline to award costs in this application in my discretion.
